name: Bali
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_quote: The P-phrase carries a single prominent phrase stress, on the last P-word. Individual P-words earlier in the P-phrase are not perceptibly stressed ... words in isolation are stressed differently from when they occur in phrase: only the phrase-final word carrying stress ... Imposition of phrase-level stress therefore involves the deletion of word-level stress everywhere except in final position.

new_statements.quote: The intonation patterns of the two are different: the verb with the contrastive FOC reading has a rising intonation and a strong stress (generally accompanied by vowel lengthening) on the penultimate syllable whereas the verb with the ANTI-TOP reading has a rather flat intonation with no such a strong stress.
new_statements.citation: Arka, I Wayan. 2003. Balinese morphosyntax: a lexical-functional approach. Pacific Linguistics 547. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics. doi:10.15144/PL-547 (NOT in the listed works; already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 pass)
new_statements.locator: p. 110 (PDF page 128), Chapter 4, discussion of examples (109)-(110); also p. 92 (p. 109) on stressable pronominals
new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File, text. The main quote is verbatim on p. 110 (p. 128, running head '110 Chapter 4', discussion of (109)-(110)): 'The intonation patterns of the two are different: the verb with the contrastive FOC reading has a rising intonation and a strong stress (generally accompanied by vowel lengthening) on the penultimate syllable whereas the verb with the ANTI-TOP reading has a rather flat intonation with no such a strong stress.' (the scanned renders FOC as 'FOe'; the compiler normalised it). Minor locator error: the second passage 'they can be stressed, as they can elsewhere' is on p. 91 (p. 109, running head 'Phrase structure 91'), not p. 92; the '92 Chapter 4' header in the txt begins the nex…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's penult record (StressTyp2 final stress): the syllable that carries the strong focus stress is the penult. It adds that the focal stress is realised with rising intonation and vowel lengthening, and that pronoun clitics are unstressed while full pronouns can bear stress. It is a syntax monograph and does not state a general word-stress rule, so it supports rather than independently establishes penultimate stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No phonology chapter and no general statement of word-stress placement; the only placement statement is incidental: under contrastive focus a verb carries strong stress, with vowel lengthening, on its penultimate syllable. Elsewhere (p. 92) full pronominals such as ida, ipun, ia, titiang 'can be stressed, as they can elsewhere', i.e. stress is a word-level property that clitics like =(n)a lack.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the statement is about focus-marked verbs, not a general rule
new_statements.identity_note: Arka & Sedeng 2018 describes Sembiran Balinese, a conservative Bali Aga (mountain) dialect of northern Bali, and contrasts it with Plains (Dataran) Balinese; it is silent on word stress in either. Arka 2003 describes Balinese generally (Plains Balinese, with high-register forms marked h.r.).

[...] 2.1.2 Fonem Suprasegmental. Sampai saat ini belum ditemukan adanya fonem suprasegmental dalam bahasa Bali. Dalam bahasa Bali dialek Nusa Penida ada kata: /mani/ : "besok" /mani:/ "kapan saja (?)"
tone_statements.translation: 10. Prosodic features, as suprasegmental phonemes, do not exist in Balinese, except for juncture between morphemes. Therefore I do not discuss them. [...] 2.1.2 Suprasegmental phonemes. Up to now no suprasegmental phoneme has been found in Balinese. In the Nusa Penida dialect of Balinese there is the word /mani/ 'tomorrow' : /mani:/ 'any time (?)'.
tone_statements.locator: p. 19, Bab II section 2.1.1 'Kesimpulan dan Saran', point 10; p. 23, section 2.1.2 'Fonem Suprasegmental'
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone and no contrastive stress: the authors find no suprasegmental phonemes in Balinese (only morpheme juncture), with a single tentative vowel-length pair reported for the Nusa Penida dialect.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all three deciding passages (final-syllable rule p.106, suffix shift p.107, phrase-stress/deletion passage p.108) are verbatim in the Clynes 1995 PDF we hold/txt at the stated pages (pp.123-125). (2) Deciding source: a 393-pp ANU PhD thesis (1995) whose Part I is a full phonology with a dedicated stress section; it is the most detailed first-hand account of Balinese stress that exists — Glottolog lists no later phonology, Ward 1973 is older, Barber/Kersten are dismissed by Clynes himself, and web search found no JIPA Illustration or instrumental study; five open items downloaded now (Kaufman & Himmelmann draft, Arka 2003 PL-547, Arka & Sedeng 2018, van Zanten & Goedemans 2007, Himmelmann 2018) are all silent or merely consistent. (3) Coding 'final, fixed-dominant, not strict' matches the source. One wording point for the record, not a reclassify: the correction line says the s

tone.quote: 1) Wat hier van de korte uitspraak der a in de derde lettergreep van achteren gezegd is, geldt evenzeer van de overige klinkers en moet hieruit verklaard worden, dat in deze taal de nadruk gewoonlijk op de tweede syllabe valt, waardoor de voorgaande open of gesloten klinker van zelf eenigsins korter wordt uitgesproken. In woorden, waarbij de klemtoon verplaatst is, b. v. pàboewan (van paboewahan) en pàbijan (in plaats van pabéjan), blijft deze klinker dan ook lang.
tone.locator: p. 14 footnote 1, continued at the foot of p. 15 (chapter on pronunciation, par. 50); cf. par. 54 on p. 15 ('in de voorgaande open lettergreep, wanneer de nadruk daarop valt, b. v. bèkèn, pèsan, Boelèlèng..')
tone.translation: 1) What has been said here about the short pronunciation of a in the third syllable from the end holds equally for the other vowels, and is to be explained by the fact that in this language the stress usually falls on the second syllable, so that the preceding open or closed vowel is naturally pronounced somewhat shorter. In words in which the stress has been shifted, e.g. pàboewan (from paboewahan) and pàbijan (instead of pabéjan), this vowel accordingly remains long.
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.summary: No tone statement; stress said to fall 'usually on the second syllable' (context: trisyllables, i.e. the antepenultimate vowel is shortened because it precedes the stress), with lexicalised stress shift in contracted forms.
